Wow MSM reporting on "Illegal" warrents.

Did gardaí warn judge that court order to check Gript X messages could breach journalists’ rights?

Officers were seeking videos of violence on right-wing website after attacks on officers.

An  Garda Síochána has declined to say if the District Court was told  issues of journalistic privilege could arise when a court order was  sought to access the private messages of a conservative news website as  part of an investigation into an assault on gardaí.

X,  the social media company owned by Elon Musk, revealed last week it had  informed 10 Irish users it has “successfully opposed court orders  granting government access to their data” under Section 63 of the  Criminal Justice Act 1994.

Gardaí  sought access to accounts that posted videos and other material in  relation to anti-immigration protests in Newtownmountkennedy, Co  Wicklow, last year.

Among  the accounts from which they sought to obtain private direct messages  was that of Gript, the conservative website edited by John McGuirk.

McGuirk said Gript was only told of the June 2024 application earlier this month.

He  said the garda application was an attack on the freedom of the press in  Ireland because it was an attempt to reveal Gript’s confidential  sources.

In  a 2023 Supreme Court ruling, it said a garda attempt to seize the phone  of Roscommon journalist Emmett Corcoran was not legal as gardaí had not  informed the District Court judge who granted the warrant that issues  of journalistic privilege could arise.

In December 2018, Corcoran, the editor of local newspaper The Democrat,  was among the first on the scene of a violent attack by vigilantes at a  house outside Strokestown that had been forc­ibly repossessed from a  family by agents working for KBC bank.

​The  Supreme Court said the District Court judge was not offered the  opportunity to reject the warrant based on the fundamental information  that Corcoran was a journalist and had invoked journalistic privilege.

An  Garda Síochána was found to have a responsibility to protect  journalistic sources and should have disclosed this information. The  Supreme Court said the Government should urgently legislate to address  the “systemic” problems involving the warrant issued in the case.

In  the Gript case, gardaí were seeking copies of videos posted by the site  and its private messages as part of an investigation into an alleged  assault on officers policing the sometimes violent protests in  Newtownmountkennedy.

This  week, a garda spokesman declined to say if the district court was  informed that issues of journalistic privilege could arise in seeking  Gript’s private messages.

The  spokesman said a directive was issued in January last year informing  all gardaí of the Supreme Court’s decis­ion in the Corcoran case  relating to journalistic privilege.

The spokesman said gardaí have acc­ess to legal advice from a dedicated unit.

“In  order to vindicate the rights of potential victims of crime, including  gardaí who have been verbally and physically assaulted, An Garda  Síochána has a positive obligation to obtain all available evidence  relating to particular incidents,” he said.

“At times, such evidence is procured on foot of court orders being issued by the courts to An Garda Síochána.”

He confirmed a court order relating to Gript was issued last June.

“The  decision to issue such court orders by the judiciary is a matter for  the courts,” he said. “As such submissions are made to courts by  individual investigating gardaí, that data is not currently available.
“An Garda Síochána takes the protection of the right of journalists to report freely and in safety very seriously.”

A  spokesman for Justice Minister Jim O’Callaghan declined to say if the  minister had sought a report on the matter, and said it would be  inappropriate to comment, given the independence of the gardaí and  judiciary.

The  Department of Justice said the Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill is on the  Government’s priority list for publication this year and would mean any  search warrant application made to the court would be obliged to include  notice of potential issues of privilege, where known.

The  Criminal Justice (Protection, Preservation of and Access to Data on  Information Systems) Bill 2024 is also being prepared for publication.

“It  will allow, among other things, Irish law enforcement authorities to  request, via judicial authorisation, the production of data held by  internet service providers,” the spokesman said.

“Where  questions of privilege arise, the approach taken is in line with the  Supreme Court judgment in the Corcor­an case, and consistent with the  approach taken in the Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill.”

​It  will set out that when issues of privilege arise, the judge may grant a  preservation order to protect the data pending determination by the  High Court.

Writing in The Irish Times yesterday,  TJ McIntyre, chairman of Digital Rights Ireland, said the garda attempt  to gain Gript’s private messages was “a propaganda victory for  right-wing groups”.

“The  narrative is that these investigations show ‘totalitarian over-reach’  by the Irish Government, that there is something sinister about using  this investigative power against far-right violence and that the  Government is setting out to undermine freedom of expression,” Mr  McIntyre wrote.

“Hyperbolic  as these claims are, they are given a veneer of credibility by the fact  that the law is deficient, does not adequately protect privacy of users  and does not adequately protect journalistic sources.”

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

A. “Collapse of sincerity” vs “Working constitutional speech-market” — juxtaposed refutation

Claim (Mehta): algorithms monetise performance; sincerity is dead.

Counter (law-anchored): India’s system builds, protects, and disciplines truthful communication.

Free speech spine intact: Art.19(1)(a); limits only under Art.19(2)—sovereignty, integrity (via 16th Amend., 1963), public order, decency, contempt, defamation, incitement.

Shreya Singhal (2015): struck 66A IT Act; mandated narrow tests (“incitement”, “tendency to create”). Sincerity space preserved.

Right to know fuels deliberation: PUCL v. Union (2003) & ADR (2002)—candidate disclosures as Art.19(1)(a); RTI Act 2005 operationalises truth access, not performance.

State coercion checked: Anuradha Bhasin (2020)—internet restrictions must be proportional, reasoned, reviewable. Kaushal Kishor (2023)—remedies exist for ministerial speech harm; no blanket gag on political speech.

Harmful speech contained, not chilled: Subramanian Swamy (2016) upheld criminal defamation to protect Art.21 reputation; Amish Devgan (2020) clarified hate-speech thresholds—ethics by law, not by vibe.

Platform due-diligence (not censorship): IT (Intermediary Guidelines & Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021—grievance officers, 36-hr takedown on court/LEA orders, traceability for heinous crimes; 69A IT Act blocking only via speaking orders + review (per Shreya Singhal).

Election truth-checks: Model Code of Conduct, cVIGIL, paid-news rules; ECI + SVEEP strengthen voter information.

Civic transparency expanding: Open Government Data, Proactive RTI (s.4), Social Audit (MNREGA/SSA rules)—institutionalise fact visibility.

Bottom line: The architecture prizes sincerity by rights (19(1)(a)), guardrails (19(2)), remedies (courts/RTI/ECI). The market is noisy; the constitution makes it corrigible.

text:
India clearing administrative satcom spectrum at 5% AGR (4% in notified remote/border pockets) is being framed as an open runway for Starlink.

​The regulatory fine print and unit economics tell a very different story.

​What most headlines missed, and how this truly reshapes Indian telecom:
​
1. The True Cost: A 13% Total Regulatory Toll
The 5% spectrum charge isn’t the only levy. Satcom operators must still pay the standard 8% annual telecom license fee.
A total 13% AGR levy—coupled with zero terminal subsidies (the DoT rejected TRAI’s proposal to subsidize dishes via the Digital Bharat Nidhi fund)—rules out aggressive retail price dumping.
​
2. The Rejection of the Urban Disincentive
TRAI recommended a ₹500/year surcharge per urban subscriber to force operators deep into the hinterland.
The DoT scrapped it. Why? Policing dynamic satellite spot beams across fluid administrative boundaries is technically unworkable.
This greenlights high-paying, remote enterprise pockets (mining belts, maritime vessels, defense corridors, infrastructure builds, luxury eco-resorts) to cross-subsidize expensive user terminals.
​
3. Does This Threaten Jio & Airtel's Retail Broadband? No.
​ARPU Realities: Indian fibre/5G FWA already sits at ₹500–₹1,000/month. Starlink-class terminals are ₹25,000–₹40,000. That is not a home-broadband fight in tier-1 to tier-3 towns.
​Physics & Capacity: LEO is a coverage and backhaul layer. It does not replace mass retail broadband over a dense metro.

​4. The Real Competitive Playbook
​▪️$BHARTIARTL - Built an early enterprise moat. Backed by Eutelsat OneWeb, Airtel already has licensed Indian ground stations and B2B corporate contracts ready to flip the switch.
​▪️Reliance Jio: Jio Space (partnered with SES via MEO/GEO) isn't chasing rooftop dishes; they will use satcom to backhaul remote 4G/5G cell towers where laying terrestrial fiber is economically unviable.

​Domestic Satellite Ecosystem Plays:
​▪️$NELCO (Tata Group) & Hughes India: Strong legacy enterprise and maritime satcom providers that now face direct LEO competition.
​▪️$AVANTEL & $DATAPATTNS - Base station gateways, defense RF electronics, and satellite transceivers see structural domestic demand as gateway infrastructure expands.
​
Satcom in India isn't an urban consumer price war; it’s a high-margin enterprise, defense, and cellular backhaul play.

​(Educational only. Not investment advice.)

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

The Modi Government’s growing agenda for controlling what Indians can see, read, post, critique and challenge online should concern every citizen — regardless of political affiliation.

From demanding takedowns to tightening the time available to platforms to scrutinise government notices, the direction is unmistakable: comply first, question later. India’s 2026 IT-rule changes cut the takedown window for unlawful content to just three hours, while the Government has also proposed making certain official advisories legally binding on platforms. (Reuters⁠)

That is precisely why Elon Musk’s decision to resist, scrutinise and challenge government demands rather than blindly obey every request matters.

X’s own stated policy is that requests can be challenged when they are legally defective, overly broad or appear to impermissibly burden freedom of expression. (Transparency⁠)

And that is where the real problem begins for the Modi Government.

When an independent platform refuses to become an obedient extension of the State, the State’s attempts to control the narrative become visible.

No algorithm can hide that.
No press conference can spin that.
No amount of propaganda can erase that.

According to his plea, X informed Nayan on July 27 that it was acting on a blocking order issued by the ministry under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act.

Section 69A allows the Union government to direct intermediaries to block online content in specified circumstances, including concerns related to national security, sovereignty and public order.

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)

The reel is back, and we welcome that. But the questions remain unanswered, Who ordered the blocking? Why did the order name an unrelated person? Was a periodic review conducted? Why was the reel restored? IFF will continue seeking these answers from Andhra Pradesh authorities. Journalists should not need months of litigation to learn why their public-interest reporting was censored. (10/10)
Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

IFF assisted Shamsheer and Monica in approaching the Delhi High Court. During the proceedings, Meta eventually furnished the blocking order. It revealed that the order had been issued by the Director General of Police, CID, Andhra Pradesh. But it also referred to a person entirely unconnected with the journalists or their reporting. (4/10)

The journalists withdrew the Delhi proceedings with liberty to approach the jurisdictional High Court. In August, IFF’s legal team sent a notice to the Andhra Pradesh authorities seeking periodic review under the IT Rules, a hearing for the journalists, a reasoned copy of the order and restoration of the reel. No response was received. (5/10)
